summary: Jaya Pala is the last known king of the Pala line. The name Kamarupa fades over the next century as the old kingdom breaks into regions (the end is variously dated 1100, 1140 or the 13th century).

name: Bengal's Palas take western Kamarupa
summary: Ramapala conquers the west and puts Timgyadeva in charge (c. 1110–1126). Vaidyadeva follows (c. 1126–1140) and in effect founds a separate kingdom after Kumarapala's death.

name: A “lunar dynasty” on the north bank
summary: Bhaskara, Rayarideva, Udayakarna and Vallabhadeva hold parts of Kamrup, Darrang and Sonitpur. They are known from a single 1185 inscription.

name: Bakhtiyar Khalji's army is destroyed
summary: On his way back from a failed Tibet campaign, Bakhtiyar's army is annihilated in Kamarupa. The king who defeated him is traditionally called Prithu, but that identification is disputed.

name: Iwaz Khalji and Nasiruddin Mahmud
summary: Ghiyasuddin Iwaz Khalji invades and withdraws; he is captured and killed in 1227–28. Nasiruddin Mahmud installs a tributary king in Kamarupa who loses control after 1229.

name: Sukaphaa reaches Assam
summary: After leaving Mong Mao in 1215, Sukaphaa arrives at Namrup in December 1228. The Ahom kingdom is dated from here. In the west, Sandhya takes the throne of Kamarupa in the same year.

name: Yuzbak is defeated; Kamata takes shape
summary: Ikhtiyaruddin Yuzbak, governor of Bengal, invades and is defeated and killed or captured by Sandhya. Sandhya moves the capital to Kamatapur, founding the Kamata kingdom.

name: Bahadur Shah raids Kamata
summary: Ghiyasuddin Bahadur Shah of Sonargaon raids as far as Nagaon, meeting ineffective resistance from Pratapdhwaj and the Kacharis, but keeps no territory.

name: The first Ahom–Kamata war
summary: A long war between Sukhaangphaa and the Kamata king ends in a truce. It is sealed by Sukhaangphaa's marriage to the Kamata princesses Rajani and Bhajani.

name: Mahamanikya and the Saptakanda Ramayana
summary: The Barahi king Mahamanikya rules around Nagaon and Hojai (a 1352 inscription records his grant) and sponsors Madhava Kandali's Ramayana.

name: Durlabhnarayan's court poets
summary: Under Durlabhnarayan of Kamata, poets such as Hema Saraswati and Harihara Vipra write some of the earliest Assamese literature.

name: Ilyas Shah and Sikandar Shah invade
summary: Bengal forces occupy Kamrup including Guwahati in 1356–57. Sikandar Shah then pushes to the Kopili, where Kamata, Bhuyan and Barahi forces fight him near Gachtal. A coin of 1360 carries a Kamrup mint name.

name: The Chutia kingdom appears in the record
summary: Nandi and Satyanarayana rule from Sadhayapura (Sadiya), the earliest Chutia kings known from inscriptions. Tyao Khamti's expedition against them fails (1380–87).

name: Interregnums in the Ahom kingdom
summary: Three Ahom kings are assassinated or die, and the throne stays empty for long stretches (1364–1369, 1376–1380, 1389–1397).

name: Sudangphaa restores the Ahom throne
summary: The prince raised by a Brahmin family in Habung is found and enthroned in 1397. A 1401 treaty fixes the Patkai boundary and in 1403 the capital moves to Charguwa.

name: Kamata and the Ahoms drive back Azam Shah
summary: The Kamata king, allied with Sudangphaa by marriage, expels Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah across the Karatoya. A Boko inscription shows the Sultanate held part of Kamrup for some years.

name: Bhuyan rule in Kamata
summary: After Indranarayan, the Bhuyan Arimatta seizes the throne, followed by Gajanka, Sukranka and Mriganka (dates are reconstructed).

name: The Khen dynasty
summary: Niladhwaj (1440–1460), Chakradhwaj (1460–1480) and Nilambar (1480–1498) rule from Kamatapur. Nilambar expands the kingdom into Kamrup and Darrang.

name: Two Ahom kings in quick succession
summary: Suhenphaa is speared to death in his palace in 1493; Supimphaa rules until 1497, when Suhungmung takes the throne.

name: Muzaffar Shah takes parts of Kamata
summary: The Bengal sultan conquers part of Kamata and issues coins with the title Kamata Mardan.

name: Husain Shah conquers Kamata
summary: Shah Ismail Ghazi besieges and destroys Kamatapur and captures Nilambar, ending the Khen dynasty. The Sultanate holds land up to Hajo by 1502. Dates of the conquest vary between 1498 and 1499.

name: The Bhuyans end Sultanate rule
summary: Under Harup Narayan the Assamese Bhuyans overrun Danyal's garrison about ten years after the conquest. Rule passes to the Bhuyans until the Koch rise.

name: Suhungmung annexes the Chutia kingdom
summary: Habung is taken in 1512 and Dhirnarayan is routed at Dibru in 1523. By 1524 Phrasengmung Borgohain governs Sadiya.

name: Biswa Singha founds the Koch kingdom
summary: Biswa Singha is crowned in Kamata after defeating the Baro-Bhuyans, ending the confusing interval of fragments left after the Khen.

name: Kamarupa
summary: The ancient kingdom of the Varman, Salastambha and Pala dynasties, c. 350 to 1100 CE.
notes: The traditional bounds, from the Karatoya in the west to Sadiya in the east, rest on texts; no inscription confirms them. Capitals: Pragjyotishpura, Haruppeswara (Tezpur) and Durjaya.
location: Assam, with parts of North Bengal, northern Bangladesh and Bhutan at its height

name: Kamata
summary: The successor kingdom of western Kamarupa, c. 1250 to 1498 (Sandhya to the Khen dynasty), between the Karatoya and the Barnadi.
notes: Early history is reconstructed from epigraphy and later tradition.
location: Kamrup, Goalpara and Dhubri in Assam; Cooch Behar and Jalpaiguri in West Bengal; Rangpur and northern Mymensingh in Bangladesh

name: Upper Assam
summary: The eastern Brahmaputra valley, the Ahom heartland.
also_called: Ujoni Assam; Ujani Asom; Upper Assam valley
location: The districts of Dibrugarh, Tinsukia, Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, Golaghat, Dhemaji and Lakhimpur in eastern Assam

name: Lower Assam
summary: The western Brahmaputra valley, the Kamarupa and Kamata country.
also_called: Namoni Assam; Western Assam; Namani Asom
location: Kamrup, Goalpara, Dhubri, Barpeta, Nalbari and nearby districts of western Assam

name: Brahmaputra Valley
summary: The long river valley that holds most of Assam's history.
also_called: Assam Valley; Assam valley; Brahmaputra plain

name: Brahmaputra
summary: The great river of the valley. Early texts call it Lauhitya; Assamese call it Luit.
location: Flows through Arunachal Pradesh and Assam in India, then Bangladesh

name: Kopili
summary: A north-flowing tributary of the Brahmaputra; its valley held the Davaka kingdom and later the Bhuyan heartland.
location: Karbi Anglong, Nagaon and Morigaon districts, Assam

name: Kolong
summary: A branch of the Brahmaputra; the first Borphukan's territory lay between the Brahmaputra and the Kolong, and Ahom rule reached it in the 16th century.

name: Manas
summary: After 1682 the western edge of Ahom control, held against the Mughals.

name: Barnadi
summary: The eastern boundary of Kamata and of the early Koch kingdom.

name: Karatoya
summary: The western boundary of Kamata and the traditional western boundary of Kamarupa; long the line fought over with Bengal's rulers.

name: Teesta
summary: Crossed by Bakhtiyar Khalji's army in 1206 on the road to and from Tibet.

name: Dikhou
summary: The old frontier between the Ahoms and the Kacharis in the 13th century.

name: Dihing
summary: The river of the early Ahom capitals, including Charagua.
also_called: Burhi Dihing; Buri Dihing; Dihing River
location: Tinsukia, Dibrugarh and Sivasagar districts, Assam

name: Safrai
summary: River on which the Ahom king Sutuphaa met the Chutia king in 1376.
notes: Present-day course not established in the sources read.

name: Namdang
summary: A river near Garhgaon, with a stone bridge of the Ahom period.
notes: Exact setting not re-checked.

name: Pushpabhadra
summary: River named in a Pala grant issued by Dharmapala.
notes: Present-day river not established here. A 12th-century copper plate named for it comes from the north bank, North Guwahati region; the exact location is unknown, so it is not geocoded.
location: Brahmaputra valley, Assam (exact river not established)

name: Guwahati
summary: The chief city of Lower Assam; the seat of the Borphukan after 1682 and the site of the Battle of Saraighat.

name: Pragjyotishpura
summary: The first capital of Kamarupa under the Varman dynasty, traditionally at Guwahati.
notes: Identification with Guwahati is traditional.

name: North Guwahati
summary: The north-bank town identified with Kamarupanagara, the post-Pala capital that Sandhya later left.
notes: Map point is the town, approximate.
location: Kamrup district, Assam (north bank of the Brahmaputra)

name: Kamarupanagara
summary: The capital of Kamarupa in the late Pala and post-Pala period, abandoned for Kamatapur after Sandhya defeated Yuzbak in 1257.
notes: Identified with North Guwahati.

name: Durjaya
summary: A Pala capital built or renamed by Ratnapala.
notes: The sources read disagree: one article says North Guwahati; the project's own note on Ratnapala says Hadapyaka (Tezpur) was renamed Durjaya. Identified with Tezpur (user, 2026-10-31); Haruppeswara and Hadapyaka are older names of the same town, so the map dot is under Haruppeswara. The North Guwahati reading in one article is set aside.

name: Haruppeswara
summary: The capital of the Salastambha dynasty, c. 650 to 900.

name: Karnasuvarna
summary: The capital of Shashanka, ruler of Gauda.
notes: Standard identification; not re-checked in this session. Map point is the Rangamati mounds near Chiruti, about 10 km south-west of Berhampore (Wikipedia).

name: Davaka
summary: A frontier kingdom named with Kamarupa on Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar; Kalyanavarman is said to have taken it.
notes: Standard identification; not re-checked here.

name: Nidhanpur
summary: Findspot of Bhaskaravarman's Nidhanpur copper-plate grant.
notes: Standard identification; not re-checked here. The earlier note said Moulvibazar; Wikipedia and the inscription gazetteer place the findspot in Sylhet District. Map point: locality coordinate, approximate.
location: Sylhet District, Sylhet Division, Bangladesh (Beanibazar area)

name: Umachal
summary: Findspot of the cave-temple inscription of Surendravarman for Balabhadra (5th century).
notes: Map point is the monument-level coordinate (best available).
also_called: Umachal slope of Nilachal; Umachal rock inscription
location: Slope of Nilachal Hill, Guwahati, Assam

name: Nilachal
summary: The hill of the Kamakhya temple, a sacred centre of Kamarupa.
also_called: Nilachal Hill; Nilanchal; Kamakhya Hill; Nilachal Parvat

name: Kamakhya
summary: The great Shakta temple of Kamarupa and Assam.
also_called: Kamakhya Temple; Kamakhya Devi; Kamakhya Mandir

name: Sualkuchi
summary: A Pala-period grant is named for it; today the centre of Assam's silk weaving. An 11th-century copper plate is recorded from Sualkuchi (gazetteer coordinate 26.16806, 91.57111).
location: Kamrup district, Assam (north bank of the Brahmaputra)

name: Barganga
summary: Findspot of a rock inscription of Bhutivarman (6th century). Dated c. 600 CE in the inscription gazetteer.
notes: The inscription's reading and date are disputed (Bhattasali vs Sircar). The Directorate of Archaeology, Assam places the village near Dokmoka in Karbi Anglong, not at Doboka in Nagaon as older notes had it. Map point is calculated from that description, not a surveyed GPS point; needs a field check.
also_called: Badaganga; Barganga river; Badaganga rock inscription
location: Barganga village, about 3 km south of Dokmoka, Karbi Anglong district, Assam

name: Barpanara
summary: Findspot of Indrapala's copper-plate grant. The Gauhati copper plate (11th century) is attributed to this findspot.
notes: Map point is a locality coordinate, approximate.

name: Mong Mao
summary: The Tai state from which Sukaphaa left in 1215.
notes: Some accounts place it instead in the Hukawng valley, Myanmar.
also_called: Muang Mao; Maw; Mao Lung; Mong Mao Lung
location: Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan, China

name: Mungdunshunkham
summary: 'The land of golden gardens', the Tai homeland in the Ahom chronicles.
notes: Identification with the Hukawng valley is traditional.
also_called: Mung Dun Sun Kham; Land of the Golden Gardens

name: Mungkang
summary: The Tai state beyond the Patkai that sent an invasion force in the early 15th century.
notes: Standard identification; not re-checked here.

name: Patkai Range
summary: The hills Sukaphaa crossed in 1228.
location: Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland, on the India-Myanmar border

name: Pangsau Pass
summary: The pass through which Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai in 1228.
location: Changlang district, Arunachal Pradesh, on the India-Myanmar border

name: Khamjang
summary: River crossed by Sukaphaa before the Nongnyang lake.
notes: Present-day place not established in the sources read.
location: Patkai foothills, near the border (exact place not established)

name: Nongnyang
summary: Lake where Sukaphaa left a guard in 1227 and where the 1401 treaty fixed the Patkai boundary.
notes: Present-day place not established in the sources read.
location: Patkai foothills, Upper Assam (exact place not established)

name: Namrup
summary: Where Sukaphaa arrived in December 1228; later a refuge for Jayadhwaj Singha in 1662.

name: Habung
summary: An early Ahom base and a Chutia-ruled area; where Prince Sudang was raised in hiding.
notes: The sources read give Dhakuakhana in one place and Dhemaji in another.
location: North bank of the Brahmaputra, Lakhimpur or Dhemaji district, Assam

name: Tipam
summary: An early Tai settlement area; site of the battle at Kuhiarbari in 1401 or so.
notes: Exact setting approximate.

name: Simaluguri
summary: An early Ahom settlement.
notes: Sukaphaa's site is placed 'downstream of' present Simaluguri; not re-checked.

name: Ligirigaon
summary: An early Ahom base before Charaideo.

name: Mungklang
summary: Sukaphaa's base in 1236.
notes: Sources equate it with Abhoipur; not re-checked.

name: Charaideo
summary: The sacred first capital of the Ahoms, founded in 1253, and the site of the royal moidams.
notes: Charaideo district was cut from Sivasagar in 2015. Capital c. 1253 to 1397 in the user capitals list (2026-10-31); map point from that list.

name: Charagua
summary: The Ahom capital from about 1397 to 1497, built on the Dihing.
notes: Present-day place not established in the sources read. Place fixed by the user 2026-10-31 from the village and PIN (785672); the 27.079243 N, 94.660540 E point is that village, not surveyed against the Ahom capital remains. Map point (27.084086 N, 94.644578 E) is from the user capitals list, 2026-10-31; it replaces the earlier village pin 27.079243, 94.660540 about 1.5 km away. Sources differ on the dates.

name: Garhgaon
summary: An Ahom capital from the 17th century, with the Kareng Ghar palace.
notes: District placement not re-checked. Capital from about 1539 or 1540 to 1707 in the user capitals list. Map point (26.966667 N, 94.683333 E) is from the user capitals list, 2026-10-31, used at the user's request. It lies about 8 km west of the Kareng Ghar palace point (26.9355, 94.7443), which is kept on the Kareng Ghar page; not reconciled.

name: Kareng Ghar
summary: The seven-storey palace of the Ahom kings at Garhgaon, rebuilt in brick in the 18th century.

name: Sivasagar
summary: The Ahom capital Rangpur (1699 to 1788), renamed for the Sivasagar tank dug in 1733.
notes: In Ahom scenes 'Rangpur' means this town. Kamata texts also mention Rangpur in present Bangladesh; see rangpur-bangladesh. The user capitals list gives Rangpur as capital 1707 to 1794, at the Talatal Ghar site; see rangpur-ahom. The dates above (1699 to 1788) are from the earlier source.

name: Rang Ghar
summary: The royal sports pavilion of the Ahom kings, an early 18th-century amphitheatre.
also_called: Rang Ghar; Rong Ghar; Royal sports pavilion

name: Joysagar
summary: The great tank dug by Rudra Singha in memory of his mother Joymoti, with temples on its bank.

name: Jorhat
summary: The last Ahom capital (from 1794), and the site of Lachit's maidam at Hoolungapara.
notes: Last capital 1794 to 1826 (called Dichoi in the user capitals list).

name: Hoolungapara
summary: Site of the Lachit Maidam built by Udayaditya Singha.

name: Mahgarh
summary: Where Chandrakanta Singha camped and lost to the Burmese in April 1822.
notes: Location given in the project's scene text.

name: Majuli
summary: The great river island of the Brahmaputra, a centre of Vaishnava satras.

name: Sadiya
summary: The seat of the Chutia kingdom, taken by the Ahoms in 1523-24.

name: Bengmara
summary: The seat of the Moran and Matak chiefs during the Moamoria rebellions.
notes: Identification with the Tinsukia area is approximate.

name: Saraighat
summary: Site of the great naval battle of March 1671.
location: Guwahati, Assam (the narrowest reach of the Brahmaputra)

name: Itakhuli
summary: The Mughal garrison fort retaken by the Ahoms (1667 in the project's scenes; August 1682 in other sources).
notes: The date differs between sources; one gives the fort's site as the present Deputy Commissioner's bungalow.
location: South bank of the Brahmaputra near Nilachal, Guwahati, Assam

name: Alaboi
summary: Site of the 1669 defeat in which about 10,000 Ahom soldiers died.
notes: The sources read give only 'Alaboi plains' and 'Alaboi hills near Dalbari'.
location: Near Dalbari, Assam (exact present place not established)

name: Kaliabor
summary: The seat of the Borphukan; Lachit died here in April 1672.

name: Kajali
summary: The first seat of the Borphukan and the Ahom outpost at the mouth of the Kolong; first Mughal foray in 1615.
notes: Exact site approximate.

name: Samdhara
summary: Ahom fort where the Mughal fleet was destroyed in a night attack.
notes: The Treaty of Ghilajharighat text places Samdhara on the Bharali river; the AHOM map point sits near Tezpur, which agrees. Another source mentions a Samdhara fort resisting the Mughals around 1636.
present_name: On the Bharali (Kameng) river, north bank (per the 1663 treaty text)

name: Duimunisila
summary: Place of the naval fight that stopped the Mughal advance in the early Mughal war.
notes: Present-day place not established in the sources read.

name: Ghilajharighat
summary: Where the Treaty of Ghilajharighat of January 1663 was signed after Mir Jumla's invasion.
notes: Present-day place not established in the sources read.

name: Dhubri
summary: A frontier town on the lower Brahmaputra, the western limit of Ahom control at times.

name: Nagaon
summary: A central Assam town and district, where Iwaz Khalji's army was turned back in 1226-27 (per the Gachtal inscription).

name: Dimapur
summary: The Dimasa (Kachari) capital until the 16th century, with brick walls, tanks and carved pillars.

name: Maibong
summary: The Dimasa capital after Dimapur was abandoned.

name: Kamatapur
summary: The capital of Kamata from about 1257, and of the Khen kings; destroyed in 1498.
notes: Sources place it near Cooch Behar or at Gosanimari.

name: Cooch Behar
summary: The Koch Bihar capital in the 16th century, near the old Kamatapur.

name: Gachtal
summary: Findspot of an inscription of the Sultanate wars; where allies fought Sikandar Shah in 1362. The archaeological site also yielded a copper-plate grant (11th century) and a later stone inscription (c. 1200 to 1300 CE); they are two separate records.
notes: Standard identification as given in the sources read. Map point is the official site GPS of the Government of Assam.

name: Langamaguri
summary: Where Chandivara's group of Kayastha and Brahmin families were settled by Kamata's kings.
location: North of Guwahati, Assam (exact place not established)

name: Bordowa
summary: The village of Sankardev's birth and early life, in the Bhuyan country.
notes: His birthplace is also given as Patekibari near Bhuragaon.

name: Hajo
summary: The limit of Husain Shah's conquest by 1502; later a Koch seat.

name: Rangpur (Bangladesh)
summary: Held by Dharmanarayan after the split of Kamata; not the Ahom Rangpur (Sivasagar).

name: Gaur
summary: The capital of the Bengal Sultanate and earlier Gauda.
notes: Lakhnauti was the Sultanate's regional centre near Gaur.
location: Malda district, West Bengal, on the Bangladesh border

name: Devkot
summary: The Bengal Sultanate's frontier base from which Bakhtiyar Khalji set out in 1206.
notes: Map point is the village of Devkot near Gangarampur; the medieval site is uncertain.

name: Sonargaon
summary: The eastern Bengal capital from which Bahadur Shah raided Kamata in 1321-22.
notes: Map point is the Sonargaon upazila headquarters, not the ruins.

name: Sylhet
summary: A region held by rulers claiming Kamarupa's legacy.

name: Kanauj
summary: Harsha's capital, where the great assembly of c. 643 was held.

name: Thanesar
summary: The early seat of Harsha's family.

name: Nalanda
summary: The Buddhist monastic university where Xuanzang studied.
notes: Kamarupa clay seals of the 7th century were found at Nalanda.

name: Allahabad Pillar
summary: Samudragupta's pillar inscription, the first written mention of Kamarupa.
notes: Map point is Prayagraj fort, where the pillar stands.

name: Aphsad
summary: Findspot of Adityasena's inscription, which records Mahasenagupta's defeat of Susthitavarman.
notes: District not re-checked.

name: Malwa
summary: A Gupta-period kingdom whose raid on Kamarupa is noted in the Varman story.

name: Delhi
summary: The seat of the Sultanate and then the Mughal court.

name: Kamauli
summary: Findspot of Vaidyadeva's copper-plate grant. The 12th-century plate was found in present-day Uttar Pradesh, outside Assam.
notes: Standard identification; not re-checked here. Map point is the Kamauli near Varanasi found on OpenStreetMap; not checked against the copperplate literature.

name: Ava
summary: The Burmese capital area that sent armies into Assam in 1817-1826.

name: Yandabo
summary: Where the Treaty of Yandabo (1826) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War and Burmese rule in Assam.
notes: Map point from OpenStreetMap, which puts the village in the Myingyan area of Mandalay Region.

name: Dikhowmukh
summary: Where the Dikhow river meets the Brahmaputra.
notes: From the catalogue coordinates; not otherwise checked.
location: At the mouth of the Dikhow river, Sivasagar district, Assam (approximate)

name: Singri
summary: A place on the Ahom map catalogue.
notes: Identified only from the catalogue coordinates; not otherwise checked.
location: Darrang district, Assam (approximate, from the coordinates)

name: Narayanpur
summary: A place on the Ahom map catalogue.
notes: Identified only from the catalogue coordinates; not otherwise checked.

name: Biswanath
summary: A town on the north bank of the Brahmaputra.

name: Dergaon
summary: A town in Upper Assam.

name: Auniati Satra
summary: A Vaishnava satra on Majuli.

name: Jogighopa
summary: A town on the Brahmaputra in Lower Assam.

name: Jerenga Pathar
summary: The field near Sivasagar associated with Joymoti.
notes: Location as given in the AHOM catalogue.

name: Umananda
summary: A Shiva temple on Peacock Island at Guwahati.
location: Peacock Island in the Brahmaputra, Guwahati, Assam

name: Jaintiapur
summary: The capital of the Jaintia kingdom.
notes: Present-day location from standard references; not re-checked.

name: Siva Dol
summary: The great Shiva temple on the Sivasagar tank.

name: Talatal Ghar

name: Manipur

name: Nazira

summary: A great wetland and grassland reserve south of the Brahmaputra.

summary: The capital of Nagaland, in the Naga hills.

name: Imphal
summary: The capital of Manipur.

summary: A Tai state, also called Mong Yang.
notes: Present-day name as given in the AHOM catalogue.

name: Sankosh
summary: The river that divided Koch Bihar from Koch Hajo in 1581; roughly today's Assam-West Bengal border.
location: Along the border of Assam and West Bengal, from Bhutan to the Brahmaputra system

name: Bhareli
summary: A north-bank river near Tezpur; the eastern limit of Koch Hajo, and where the 1663 treaty put the Ahom-Mughal frontier on the north bank (Samdhara on the Bharali).
notes: Spelled Bharali, Bhareli or Bhoroli in different sources.
also_called: Bharali; Bhareli; Jia Bharali; Kameng; Bhoroli
location: Arunachal Pradesh and Sonitpur district, Assam

name: Subansiri
summary: A major north-bank river; the Chutia heartland lay on it, and Koch power briefly reached it under Nara Narayan.
location: Arunachal Pradesh and Assam (Lakhimpur and Dhemaji districts)

name: Dibang
summary: An eastern river; the 'Dikshu' of the Kalika Purana is linked to it as the eastern limit of Kamarupa.
notes: Linking Dikshu to the Dibang rests on Sircar and Boruah.

The second is used because it matches the later Ahom-Kachari frontier on the Dikhow. Habung (Dhemaji) lay on the north bank from 1240, so the Brahmaputra is not a strict limit. notes: Kamrup's role (cutting the bridge and supplies) rests on Bhattacharya's account; the king 'Prithu' is a later identification (low) and the 'Kanai-Barasi-Bowa' inscription is unverified. Bakhtiyar's death is disputed (illness or assassination by Ali Mardan). Artistic reconstruction; the broken bridge and river are the subject; show no clear Kamrup army. Painting: unnamed participants; the bridge’s site and form are uncertain. Modern artistic reconstruction; clothing drawn from present-day regional dress references, not period evidence.

name: Sukaphaa Departs Mong Mao
summary: Prince Sukaphaa leaves his ancestral kingdom of Mong Mao following a succession dispute, leading 9,000 followers, noblemen, priests (Deodhais), horses, and two royal war elephants across Upper Burma towards Assam.

name: Iwaz Khalji Is Turned Back Near Nagaon
summary: Bengal's Sultan Ghiyasuddin Iwaz Khalji campaigns up the valley as far as the Nagaon region, where the Gachtal inscription records his defeat. Coins suggest he may have reached Guwahati before returning to Lakhnauti, where Nasiruddin Mahmud captures and kills him.
notes: The reach of his campaign is disputed (Nagaon vs Guwahati). Artistic reconstruction; river fog and flooded fields; a small mounted force. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Nasiruddin Mahmud Crosses into Kamrup
summary: The Delhi prince Nasiruddin Mahmud, governor of Bengal, crosses through Jalpaiguri into Kamrup. The local king fortifies against him but is killed (an assassination plot is reported). A successor, Sandhya, is installed on condition of paying tribute.
notes: King's name 'Prithu' comes from later tradition (low). Sandhya's installation is the Wikipedia/Sarkar reconstruction (medium). Artistic reconstruction; show defences and the invaders' crossing; avoid portraying a named king. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Crossing the Patkai Hills
summary: Sukaphaa and his vanguard conquer the steep, dense subtropical mountain rainforests of the Patkai Range (Pangsau Pass), outmaneuvering hostile hill tribes and arriving at Khamjang on the border of Assam.

name: Negotiation and Settlement with Naga Chiefs
summary: Descending into Namrup, Sukaphaa establishes firm frontier peace through tactical deterrence and diplomatic accords with eastern Naga chieftains.

name: First View of the Brahmaputra Valley
summary: Sukaphaa and scouts view the immense, fertile Brahmaputra River plain ('Mung Dun Sun Kham' - Country of Golden Gardens), recognizing its potential for wet-rice cultivation.

name: Sukaphaa Enters the Assam Valley
summary: Formal arrival of Sukaphaa's royal entourage in the plains of Upper Assam along the Dihing river basin in 1228 CE, officially inaugurating the 600-year Ahom Dynasty.
notes: Arrival at Namrup in December 1228. In the same year Sandhya took the throne of Kamarupa.

name: Establishment of the First Tai Settlements
summary: Initial settlements established at Tipam, Habung, and Shimolguri; stilt houses (Rwan-hon) constructed and virgin floodplains cleared for agriculture.

name: The Sacred Promontory of Charaideo
summary: The sacred royal compound and ancestral temples at Charaideo, the spiritual center and eternal resting place of Ahom royalty.

name: Institution of the Supreme Offices of Burhagohain and Borgohain
summary: Sukaphaa institutes the Great Council of Nobles: Thaomung Klinglunmang (Burhagohain) and Thaomung Kangngan (Borgohain), forming a hereditary prime-ministerial council.

name: Samudrapala Visits a Religious Establishment
summary: Samudrapala, known from the Ambari inscription, visits a religious house whose residents he supports.
notes: The original inscription edition was not inspected; site, sect and ritual are unresolved. Not a later Ekasarana sattra. Modern artistic reconstruction; clothing drawn from present-day regional dress references, not period evidence.

name: Matrimonial Alliances with Borahi and Moran Rulers
summary: Sukaphaa adopts an assimilative policy by establishing matrimonial bonds with the indigenous Moran chief Bodousa and the Borahi king Thakumtha, marrying local princesses and integrating them into court governance.

name: Sandhya Stops the Tribute
summary: After Nasiruddin dies in 1229 and Bengal falls into confusion, Sandhya stops paying tribute, pushes the Muslim garrisons out, and extends his control to the Karatoya. He takes the title Gaudesvara after raiding across it.
notes: Details (Gaur raid, the title) rest on Sarkar and Acharyya via summaries; reconstructed. Artistic reconstruction; a royal court receives news; riverside garrison being withdrawn. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Introduction of Advanced Wet-Rice Cultivation (Sali Kheti)
summary: Introduction of advanced Tai hydraulic techniques, dyke bunding, canal irrigation, and deep-water transplanted Sali rice, producing an agricultural surplus.

name: Founding and Construction of the Sacred Capital at Charaideo
summary: In 1253 CE, Sukaphaa establishes the permanent royal capital at Charaideo (Che-Rai-Doi), consecrated with sacred Tai Phuralong rituals and ancestral invocations.

name: Writing of the First Ahom Buranji (Royal Chronicles)
summary: Sukaphaa decrees that royal scribes and priests record every event, battle, decree, and genealogy on Sanchi bark (agarwood paper), establishing Assam's Buranji tradition.

name: The Royal Court of Sukaphaa
summary: Convening of the sovereign assembly at Charaideo; state administration organized with local leaders integrated, establishing a harmonious multi-ethnic polity.

name: Yuzbak Occupies an Empty Kamarupanagara
summary: Malik Ikhtiyaruddin Yuzbak crosses the Karatoya near Goraghat, marches through Goalpara and enters the Kamarupa capital, which Sandhya has evacuated. There is little resistance ahead of him and effective resistance behind him. Yuzbak is said to have built the first mosque in Assam and had the khutbah read.
notes: Route per Sarkar. The mosque and khutbah claim is in the Wikipedia summary only. Artistic reconstruction; an empty but rich capital, invaders' camp, hills in the distance. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Sandhya Floods the Plain
summary: Sandhya retreats to the hills and, by tradition, dams a hill stream; when the spring rains come he releases the water and floods the plain, then cuts the invaders' supply line. A guide offers a shorter route through the foothills; the army is trapped in a narrow valley and destroyed. Yuzbak is captured (executed, July 1257) or dies of wounds.
notes: Strongest scene for 'geography beats armies'. The dam is Tradition; the flood and the supply cut are consistent across summaries. Yuzbak's death is disputed. Artistic reconstruction; flooded paddy, boats, soldiers on small high ground. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Sandhya Becomes Kamateswara at Kamatapur
summary: Sandhya moves his capital west from North Guwahati to Kamatapur, a more defensible site across rivers, and styles himself Kamateswara. Kamarupa becomes Kamata.
notes: Reconstructed; sources place Kamatapur near Cooch Behar or at Gosanimari. Artistic reconstruction; earth-and-brick rampart rising, river moat, new capital under construction; no stone citadel. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Institution of Royal Moidams (Pyramidal Earth Tumuli)
summary: Upon Sukaphaa's demise in 1268 CE, the tradition of building subterranean vaulted brick/stone chambers covered by hemispherical earthen mounds (Moidams) begins at Charaideo.

name: Accession and Court Assembly of Suteuphaa
summary: Sukaphaa's eldest son assumes the golden throne and addresses the council of ministers to set aggressive policies for western border expansion.

name: Frontier Standoff on the Dikhou River
summary: Ahom expanding settlements encounter the Kachari Kingdom's eastern outpost along the Dikhou River.

name: Skirmishes on the Ahom-Kachari Frontier
summary: Military clashes between Ahom warriors and Kachari troops over control of fertile grazing and cultivation tracts along the Dikhou.

name: Diplomatic Negotiations with the Kachari King
summary: Suteuphaa sends envoys to avoid destructive protracted war, initiating bilateral talks with the Kachari monarch.

name: Demarcation of the Dikhou River Boundary
summary: Formal treaty demarcating the Dikhou River as the permanent mutual frontier between the Ahoms and Kacharis.

name: Conspiracy of the Eastern Naga Clans
summary: Highland Naga chieftains withhold promised tributes and plot coordinated raids on Ahom valley villages.

name: Suteuphaa Marshals the Royal Army
summary: King Suteuphaa mobilizes an expeditionary army equipped with iron-tipped arrows, daos, and war shields into the foothills.

name: The Fierce Battle of the Naga Hills
summary: Ahom forces fight intense uphill engagements against fortified Naga hill positions, defeating hostile warriors in dense jungle terrain.

name: Naga Submission and Tribute Offering
summary: Defeated Naga chiefs travel to the royal court at Charaideo to kneel, submit oaths of loyalty, and pay tribute in salt, iron, and cloths.

name: Consolidation of the Dikhou Frontier
summary: Peaceful agrarian settlements flourish across the pacified Dikhou frontier, securing Upper Assam's borders.

name: Administrative Division of the Realm
summary: Subinphaa formally partitions administrative jurisdiction and subjects into two equal domains under the Burhagohain and Borgohain.

name: Dual Provincial Governance by Gohains
summary: Burhagohain administers the northern/eastern territory while Borgohain administers the southern/western territory with autonomous judicial authority.

name: Large-scale Swamp Reclamation and Bunding
summary: Large-scale drainage canals, dykes, and earthen bunds constructed across alluvial marshlands to open vast new paddy fields.

name: Outbreak of the First Ahom-Kamata War
summary: King Sukhangphaa leads an offensive against Raja Durlabhanarayana of Kamata, seeking westward expansion into Lower Assam.

name: Frontier Battle with Kamata Forces
summary: A pitched riverine engagement between Ahom war flotillas and Kamata defensive troops along the Lower Assam river passes.

name: Military Stalemate in the Kamata Campaign
summary: After prolonged fighting and sieges without either side securing a decisive victory, both monarchs recognize mutual exhaustion.

name: Ahom-Kamata Royal Matrimonial Treaty
summary: Peace concluded by the marriage of Kamata Princess Rajani (Durlabhanarayana's daughter) to Sukhangphaa, sealing durable inter-kingdom peace.
notes: Wikipedia (Sukhaangphaa) dates the end of the war to 1324, against c. 1308 here; it names both princesses, Rajani and Bhajani.

name: Birth of Prince Chao Pulai
summary: Princess Rajani gives birth to Prince Chao Pulai, tying the royal lineages of Kamata and Ahom together.

name: The Kacharis Turn Back Bahadur Shah
summary: Ghiyasuddin Bahadur Shah of Sonargaon moves up the old Brahmaputra and raids as far as Nagaon. Pratapdhwaj of Kamata's resistance is ineffective, but Kachari forces repel the sultan with heavy losses.
notes: Low confidence; single-source summary. Bahadur Shah was killed by Muhammad Tughlaq in 1327–28. Artistic reconstruction; river boats and Kachari warriors at a ford. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Durlabhnarayan and Dharmanarayan Divide the Kingdom
summary: After a succession dispute between cousins, a settlement splits Kamata: Durlabhnarayan keeps the western core including Kamatapur and Dharmanarayan keeps Rangpur and Mymensingh.
notes: Reconstructed; exact dates unknown. Rulers' dates in the CSV are 'reconstructed'. Artistic reconstruction; a council of ministers and Brahmin witnesses. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Chao Pulai's Revolt and Alliance with Kamata
summary: Chao Pulai disputes the succession of his half-brother Sukhrangphaa and conspires with maternal Kamata envoys for military support.

name: Fraternal Reconciliation Between Sukhrangphaa and Chao Pulai
summary: Rather than shedding fraternal blood, Sukhrangphaa welcomes Chao Pulai back into the court and effects complete reconciliation.

name: Appointment of Chao Pulai as Governor of Sadiya
summary: King Sukhrangphaa invests Chao Pulai with governorship of the critical eastern frontier outpost of Sadiya.

name: Chandivara's Fourteen Families Settle at Langamaguri
summary: Under the treaty between the two kings, Chandivara's group of seven Kayastha and seven Brahmin families (traditionally refugees from Kannauj) is settled at Langamaguri near Guwahati; later they move to Bordowa with royal support. Sankardev descends from this line.
notes: On Neog's reading; Amalendu Guha instead derives the Bhuyans from local landed intermediaries. Present as one view. Artistic reconstruction; families arriving by boat, with household goods, scribes and priests; Bhuyan costume direction from research/ahom/agent-guidance.md. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Hema Saraswati Recites the Prahlada Charita
summary: At the court of Durlabhnarayan, the poet Hema Saraswati recites the Prahlada Charita, regarded as the earliest known poem in Assamese; Harihara Vipra is another court poet.
notes: Dating of the poets is uncertain. Artistic reconstruction; palm-leaf or sanchi-pat manuscript, a lamp-lit hall, listening courtiers. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Madhav Kandali Writes the Saptakanda Ramayana
summary: At the command of Mahamanikya, a Barāha/Borahi king of the Nagaon–Morigaon–Hojai region, the poet Madhav Kandali translates the Sanskrit Ramayana into Assamese verse; the Lankākānda states this patronage.
notes: The poet's own statement in the Lankākānda is the evidence for Mahamanikya (medium). Mahamanikya's dynastic label varies (Barāha vs Borahi-Kachari). Artistic reconstruction; a poet at work with a manuscript; avoid temple architecture. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Ilyas Shah Takes Guwahati
summary: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah of Bengal comes up the Brahmaputra through northern Mymensingh, enters Kamata's core and takes Guwahati. A coin dated 1357–59 minted at 'Chawlistan urf Kamrup' suggests occupation. He dies about November 1357.
notes: Coin evidence (medium). Kamata was weakened by Ahom and Kachari pressure and a breakaway chieftain (1329). Artistic reconstruction; river fleet, fort at Guwahati, hills on the horizon. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Sikandar Shah Met at Gachtal
summary: Sikandar Shah advances to the Kopili river, where Mahamanikya, Indranarayan of Kamata and the Bhuyan chiefs fight him at Gachtal near Nagaon.
notes: The outcome is not stated in the sources found; do not paint a decisive victory. Date flagged 'citation needed'. Artistic reconstruction; allied levies on the river bank, no winner shown. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Interregnum After the Death of Sukhrangphaa
summary: With no acceptable heir after Sukhrangphaa's death, the throne stays empty for five years and the Burhagohain and Borgohain rule. It is the first of three interregnums before 1397.
notes: Modern artistic reconstruction using project character sheets; setting, architecture and staging are interpretive. Empty royal seat and unnamed ministers; the deceased Sukhrangphaa is not depicted alive.

name: Arimatta Seizes the Throne
summary: The Bhuyan Arimatta overthrows the weakened Indranarayan; his successors Gajanka, Sukranka and Mriganka hold Kamata until about 1440.
notes: Reconstructed; the Bhuyan interregnum has no firm narrative. Artistic reconstruction; a palace hall, armed Bhuyan retainers. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Safrai River Diplomatic Peace Summit
summary: King Sutuphaa meets the Chutia monarch on the Safrai river for joint festivities and peace negotiations to resolve frontier friction.

name: Betrayal and Assassination of King Sutuphaa
summary: During a boat excursion on the Safrai river, the Chutia king treacherously assassinates Sutuphaa aboard the barge, triggering centuries of bitter warfare.

name: First Ministerial Interregnum
summary: Following Sutuphaa's treacherous assassination, the Burhagohain and Borgohain rule jointly for four years due to the absence of an acceptable adult royal prince.
notes: Wikipedia counts three interregnums (1364–1369, 1376–1380, 1389–1397), so this is the second.

name: Tyao Khamti's Failed Expedition Against the Chutias
summary: Nandi and Satyanarayana rule the Chutia kingdom from Sadhayapura (Sadiya), the earliest Chutia kings known from inscriptions. Tyao Khamti's campaign against them fails.
notes: Modern artistic reconstruction using project character sheets; setting, architecture and staging are interpretive. The river withdrawal and opposing Chutia ruler are illustrative, not a documented personal confrontation; campaign dates vary.

name: Banishment of the Pregnant Younger Queen
summary: While King Tyao Khamti is away battling Chutias, his jealous Chief Queen falsely accuses the beloved younger queen and sentences her to be cast adrift on a raft down the Brahmaputra.

name: Birth of Prince Sudang in Habung Village
summary: The banished pregnant queen washes ashore at Habung and is sheltered by a pious Brahmin family; she gives birth to prince Sudang before passing away.

name: Assassination of King Tyao Khamti
summary: Disgusted by Tyao Khamti's acquiescence in the murder of his innocent queen and arbitrary rule, nobles and citizens revolt and assassinate the king.

name: Second Ministerial Interregnum
summary: Ministers Burhagohain and Borgohain hold executive power for eight years following the assassination of Tyao Khamti while searching for the exiled royal prince.
notes: Wikipedia counts three interregnums (1364–1369, 1376–1380, 1389–1397), so this is the third.

name: Prince Sudang Raised in Brahmin Household
summary: Prince Sudang grows up oblivious to his royal identity, tending cattle and studying Sanskrit scriptures alongside Brahmin children at Habung.

name: A Land Grant at Sadhayapuri
summary: At Sadhayapuri, Satyanarayana issues the Dhenukhana copper-plate land grant, naming his father Nandi. Dated 1392, it is among the earliest dated records of the Chutia kingdom.
notes: The epigraphic attribution reported in the checked sources identifies Satyanarayana as issuer and Nandi genealogically; the illustration does not assume joint issue. The exact ceremony and plate lettering are artistic reconstructions.

name: Vaishnava Brahmins at the Chutia Court
summary: Vaishnava Brahmins reach the Chutia court and compose genealogies linking its kings to Krishna’s family, while ranking them below themselves.

name: Kamata and the Ahoms Drive Back Azam Shah
summary: The Kamata king, allied with Sudangphaa by marriage, drives Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah of Bengal back across the Karatoya. A Boko inscription shows the Sultanate held part of Kamrup for some years.
notes: Modern artistic reconstruction using project character sheets; setting, architecture and staging are interpretive. Exact chronology and Ahom military participation are uncertain; the Sultan at the ford is an illustrative reconstruction. Sudangphaa is not shown in battle.

name: Sudangphaa Identity Confirmation
summary: Official confirmation of royal bloodline presented to Prince Sudang at Habung by council messengers.

name: Ministers Discover the Hidden Prince Sudang at Habung
summary: After eight years of search, the Burhagohain's emissaries locate the rightful heir Prince Sudang living as an ordinary cowherd at Habung.
notes: Thao Cheoken found the prince; the Burhagohain brought him to Charaideo.

name: Triumphant Royal Return of Sudang to Charaideo
summary: Prince Sudang is escorted in state barge flotillas up the Brahmaputra to Charaideo accompanied by his Brahmin foster-family.

name: Coronation of Sudangphaa
summary: Grand accession ceremony where Prince Sudang ascends the throne taking the Tai title Chao Siu-Dang-Pha.

name: The Reign of Bamuni Konwar
summary: Sudangphaa rewards his Brahmin foster father and brothers with high court offices, inaugurating Hindu Brahminical influence.

name: Institution of the Singari-Gharutha Coronation
summary: Sudangphaa inaugurates the sacred Singari-gharutha ceremony, ascending a raised platform of Singari timber, washing in sacred waters, and killing a bull/buffalo.

name: The Feast Trap for the Tipam Conspirators
summary: Early in his reign the Tipam chiefs plot against the young king. Sudangphaa invites the conspirators to a feast and has them killed.
notes: Modern artistic reconstruction using project character sheets; setting, architecture and staging are interpretive.

name: Harmonious Synthesis of Tai and Hindu Vedic Rituals
summary: Court ceremonies conduct Vedic homa rituals alongside traditional Tai worship of Somdeo and Me-Dam-Me-Phi ancestor rites.

name: Matrimonial Alliance with Bhuyan Chieftains
summary: Sudangphaa secures stability across the north bank by establishing marriage ties with powerful Baro-Bhuyan chieftains.

name: Sudangphaa Repels the Mong Kawng Invasion
summary: The rival claimant Tai Sulai returns with a Mong Kawng (Mungkang) army led by the defector Tasim Pou. Sudangphaa meets it near Kuhiarbari in the Tipam country and defeats it, though he is lightly wounded by a spear.
notes: Modern artistic reconstruction using project character sheets; setting, architecture and staging are interpretive.

name: Treaty of the Patkai Boundary at Nongnyang Lake
summary: Ahom and Mong Kawng envoys swear a treaty by Nongnyang lake fixing the Patkai range as the border between the two kingdoms. The boundary holds for centuries.
notes: Nongnyang lake as the treaty site follows Gait, A History of Assam; Wikipedia gives only the Patkai boundary. Modern artistic reconstruction using project character sheets; setting, architecture and staging are interpretive. Painting depicts the two negotiating commanders; Sudangphaa is not physically shown.

name: Lakshminarayana’s Ghilamara Grant
summary: Lakshminarayana issues a copper-plate land grant, later found at Ghilamara.

name: Nangchukham Borgohain Marches on Kamata
summary: Tai Sulai flees to Kamata. Sudangphaa's commander Nangchukham Borgohain invades, and the Kamata king, also pressed by Bengal, makes peace and gives a daughter in marriage to Sudangphaa.
notes: Chronology of the Kamata episode is undated and disputed. Modern artistic reconstruction using project character sheets; setting, architecture and staging are interpretive.

name: Administrative Centralization at Charagua
summary: Constructs the new capital city Charagua on the Dihing river to better oversee burgeoning agricultural lands and trade routes.

name: Cultural Renaissance and Literary Patronage
summary: Sudangphaa patronizes both Tai chroniclers and Sanskrit scholars, fostering bilingualism and literary learning in court.

name: The Brick Fort at Bhismaknagar
summary: At the foot of the Mishmi hills a fortified city of fired brick and stone rises, with walls about 4.5 m high, a palace complex of three halls and several tanks. A brick bearing Lakshminarayana’s name suggests it was his capital.
notes: The name Bhismaknagar is modern (1928 gazetteer), from the Rukmini legend. Excavation has been limited. Official site chronologies differ from the simplified royal association; the ruler presence and lost upper buildings in the illustration are interpretive, not an excavated complete plan.

name: Peaceful Reign of Sujanphaa
summary: Sujanphaa preserves external peace and internal order across Upper Assam for fifteen unbroken years.

name: Consolidation Under Suphakphaa
summary: Son of Sujanphaa; a steady seventeen-year reign promoting trade, agricultural stability, and peace with neighboring hill tribes.

name: Durlabhnarayana’s Grant at Sadiya
summary: Durlabhnarayana issues the Sadiya-Chepakhowa copper-plate grant.

name: The Golden Forty-Nine-Year Peace of Susenphaa
summary: One of the longest reigns in Ahom annals; nearly five decades of uninterrupted agricultural and population growth.

name: Kanta Nath Rises as Niladhwaj, First of the Khen Kings
summary: A man of humble origin, Kanta Nath, rises to found the Khen dynasty as Niladhwaj, and rules from Kamatapur.
notes: Origin stories conflict: a poor boy from Taluk Jambari (Gosani Mangala) vs a Tripura migrant. Ethnicity uncertain. Artistic reconstruction; coronation of a local chief; keep costume modest. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: A Brick Wall for Kechaikhati
summary: Mukta Dharmanarayana, a Chutia prince, builds the brick wall of the shrine of the goddess Kechaikhati (Dikkaravasini) on the Paya river, served by Deori priests. A later copper roof gives the temple its name, Tamreswari.
notes: The copper roof is described in a 1711 chronicle; human sacrifice there is reported, mostly from later accounts.

name: A Bhuyan Boyhood at Alipukhuri
summary: The orphaned boy Sankara (later Sankardev), raised by his grandmother Khersuti in a chief Baro-Bhuyan family near Bordowa, starts school under Mahendra Kandali at about age 12.
notes: Birthplace (Alipukhuri or Patekibari) and birth year (1449 or 1479–84) are disputed. Artistic reconstruction; a village house with a courtyard and a guru's tol. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Tangshu Naga Raids on Lowland Settlements
summary: Tangshu Naga warriors raid eastern border villages, looting grain stores and capturing lowland subjects.

name: Smiths and Salt Wells of Sadiya
summary: Chutia blacksmiths, bell-metal workers and goldsmiths, and the salt springs at Borhat, make the kingdom one of the most productive of the valley.
notes: A general scene; scholars call the Chutias the most advanced tribal polity of the 15th-century valley, but details are disputed.

name: Susenphaa's Punitive Tangshu Campaign
summary: Susenphaa personally leads an army into the rugged Tangshu hills, encircling rebel villages and cutting off mountain passes.

name: Submission and Tribute of the Tangshu Chiefs
summary: Defeated Tangshu leaders present offerings of swords, amber, and mountain goods, swearing eternal peace with the Ahom throne.

name: Sankardev Stages the Chihna Yatra
summary: Young Sankardev stages a dance-drama, the Chihna Yatra, the first of the plays and performances that grow into Ankiya Naat and the satra theatre tradition.
notes: Tradition places it around 1468 at Bordowa; no date was found in the sources checked. Generated artistic reconstruction, 2026-10-29; reference roles, historical uncertainties and prompt recorded in research/completion-2026-10-29. Revised 2026-10-31: user-directed daylight village-road mobile narrative-cloth display, using the project Sankardev sheet and Vrindavani Vastra textile as visual references. The LACMA textile is dated circa 1570 and is not evidence of the actual earlier Chihna Yatra prop; processional staging is interpretive. See research/completion-2026-10-29/chihna-yatra-daylight-revision.md.

name: Erection of Charaideo Boundary Stones
summary: Inscribed stone monoliths erected around the holy hills of Charaideo to permanently safeguard the royal necropolis.

name: Nilambar's Kamatapur
summary: The Khen king Nilambar rules from the great fortified capital at Kamatapur (Gosanimari): earth-and-brick ramparts, gates, moats and royal compounds.
notes: Gosanimari is the usual identification. Claims of wide conquest are uncited. Artistic reconstruction; an establishing view of the fortified capital; no stone or temple architecture. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: The Battle of Turung Against the Kacharis
summary: Ahom forces clash fiercely with Kachari armies near the Dikhou; Ahom army suffers a tactical reverse leading to temporary tribute concessions.

name: Peace Settlement with the Kacharis
summary: Suhenphaa concludes peace with the Kachari king through tribute of royal princesses and elephants, stabilizing the southern flank.

name: Muzaffar Shah's Coins: Kamata Mardan
summary: Bengal's Sultan Shamsuddin Muzaffar Shah takes parts of Kamata and mints coins carrying the title 'Kamata Mardan' (conqueror of Kamata).
notes: Coin evidence (medium). Artistic reconstruction; a mint scene with a die-stamp and coins; or the sultan's officers in a captured town. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Tangshu Ambush of Borgohain Khenphung
summary: During a patrol in the eastern hill tracts, Borgohain Khenphung is ambushed by hostile Tangshu warriors but manages a fighting retreat.

name: Suhenphaa's Inspection of Palace Works
summary: King Suhenphaa walks unescorted among workmen to inspect new wooden palace structures at Charagua.

name: Assassination of King Suhenphaa
summary: Turung palace laborers conceal weapons and spear King Suhenphaa to death inside the palace under cover of darkness.

name: Royal Inquest and Execution of Suhenphaa's Assassins
summary: Supimphaa convenes a tribunal, identifies the conspirators behind his father's murder, and executes them publicly.

name: Supimphaa Exiles Pregnant Queen to the Nagas
summary: Due to malicious palace gossip, Supimphaa banishes his pregnant queen to the village of a loyal Naga chief.

name: Birth of Konseng in the Naga Foothills
summary: The exiled queen gives birth to prince Konseng among the Nagas, raised in mountain traditions before returning to court.

name: Sachipatra's Grievance
summary: The Brahmin minister Sachipatra, whose son was executed by Nilambar for an affair with the queen, goes to Husain Shah's court and urges him to invade.
notes: Tradition (low): a story that explains the invasion, not firm evidence. Mark clearly as legend in the viewer. Artistic reconstruction; a Brahmin petitioner at a Gaur court. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: The Siege of Kamatapur
summary: Shah Ismail Ghazi, sent by Alauddin Husain Shah, besieges the fort of Kamatapur and destroys the city. Nilambar is imprisoned and the Khen dynasty ends.
notes: Dates conflict (siege from c. 1493; fall 1498; expedition 1499). Army sizes are uncited. Artistic reconstruction; river-borne army, earth ramparts, defenders on the walls. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Danyal Governs from Hajo
summary: Husain Shah's conquest reaches Hajo by 1502; his son Shahzada Danyal governs the conquered region. Husain Shah's coins call him 'conqueror of Kamru, Kamata, Jajnagar and Urisa' and a stone at Malda records the victory.
notes: Completion date from Sarkar (via summary). Artistic reconstruction; an administrative court with Bengali officials; Hajo's riverside. Modern artistic reconstruction, not evidence of appearance or dress.

name: Konseng's Return and Presentation to King Suhungmung
summary: Grown into a stalwart warrior, Konseng is brought from the Naga village to Bakata; Suhungmung acknowledges him as half-brother of royal blood.

name: Creation of the Office of Barpatragohain
